Dead
DED
adj. / n.
Old English dēad, the state of having life cease. In the New Testament the KJV’s ordinary adjective for corpses and for the spiritually lifeless is Greek nekros (G3498), tagged on the verses below in the verse-cache. The noun-cluster death is treated at the companion entry; this page is the adjective and the company of the dead.

Biblical Definition

Dead in Scripture is not a metaphor looking for a feeling. It names a real cessation, then uses that cessation as the measure of every lesser death. Physically, the dead are those whose life has ceased: the dead, small and great, stand before God (Rev 20:12), and the dead shall be raised incorruptible (1 Cor 15:52). Spiritually, the unregenerate are dead in trespasses and sins (Eph 2:1) until God quickens them — not nearly-alive, not seeking, not wounded but still climbing, but dead, as Lazarus was dead until the Lord cried come forth. Morally and ecclesiastically, a thing may keep the name of life while being dead: Sardis had a name that thou livest, and art dead (Rev 3:1); faith that will not work is dead, being alone (Jas 2:17); the conscience that still offers the old Levitical round is occupied with dead works (Heb 9:14). Union with Christ adds a fourth use that must not be collapsed into the first three: the believer is to reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom 6:11). That death is real — the old man crucified with Christ — and it is not annihilation of the body, nor a mood of self-loathing, but a change of dominion. Christ’s own word holds the whole doctrine together: I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live (John 11:25). The dictionary therefore refuses every reading that treats dead as mere poetry. Physical death is the wages of sin; spiritual death is the estate of Adam’s race apart from regenerating grace; the second death is the lake of fire; and the only resurrection unto life is in the Son.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DEAD as deprived or destitute of life; also, in a state of spiritual death, void of grace, lying under the power of sin; and as the noun, dead men, or the state of the dead.

expand to see more

DEAD, a. — Deprived or destitute of life; that state of a being, animal or vegetable, in which the organs of motion and life have ceased to perform their functions. The men are dead who sought thy life (Ex 4:19).

DEAD, a. — In a state of spiritual death; void of grace; lying under the power of sin. Thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead (Rev 3:1). Not proceeding from spiritual life; not producing good works; as, faith without works is dead (Jas 2:17). Proceeding from corrupt nature; as dead works (Heb 9:14).

DEAD, n. — The dead signifies dead men. Ye shall not make cuttings for the dead (Lev 19:28). Also the state of the dead: This is John the Baptist; he is risen from the dead (Matt 14:2).

Key Scripture

Ephesians 2:1 — "And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;"

Romans 6:11 — "Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord."

James 2:17 — "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone."

Revelation 20:12 — "And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works."

John 11:25 — "Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:"

Modern Corruption

Dead is corrupted when spiritual death is reduced to a mood, when annihilationism erases the second death, when cheap grace calls a fruitless profession living faith, and when death-of-God and therapeutic registers treat the word as style rather than judgment and resurrection.

expand to see more

The first corruption is to make dead in trespasses and sins mean merely discouraged, unfulfilled, or “dead inside” as an aesthetic. Ephesians 2 is not a wellness diagnosis. It is total inability: the unregenerate man does not cooperate his way into life; God quickens the dead. Semi-Pelagian and decisionist revivalism both refuse this. They need a sinner who is wounded but still climbing. Scripture gives a corpse that only Christ raises.

The second corruption is annihilationism, which denies eternal conscious punishment and therefore empties the dead of Revelation 20. The dead stand; the dead are judged; the second death is not a fade-to-black. Universalism and every scheme that pretends the lake of fire will empty likewise refuse the verdict. The recovery is the creed: bodily resurrection of the just and the unjust, final judgment, heaven for the redeemed, hell for the unredeemed.

The third corruption is a fruitless profession that still claims faith. James does not overthrow justification by faith alone; he names a faith that is not faith — dead, being alone. Rome answers with justifying works. Cheap grace answers with a profession that never obeys. The Reformed confession keeps both ends: the sinner is justified by the imputed righteousness of Christ, received by faith alone; that same faith, being living, works. Sardis is the ecclesiastical form of the same lie: a name that thou livest, and art dead.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English dēad. NT adjective in the verses below is Greek nekros (G3498), tagged in the KJV verse-cache at Eph 2:1, Rom 6:11, Jas 2:17, Rev 3:1, Rev 20:12, 1 Cor 15:52. The noun death (Hebrew māwet H4194; Greek thanatos G2288) is the companion entry; this page does not invent further Strong’s numbers beyond those tags and that existing cluster.

expand to see more

Greek nekros (G3498) — dead, a corpse; physically dead and spiritually dead (Eph 2:1; Rom 6:11; Jas 2:17; Rev 3:1; Rev 20:12; 1 Cor 15:52; Matt 8:22).

Greek apothnēskō (G599) — to die; John 11:25, though he were dead, yet shall he live.

Hebrew māwet (H4194) and Greek thanatos (G2288) — death, already treated at the death entry; cited here as the noun-cluster, not as a new number guessed for every OT occurrence of dead.

Old English dēad — destitute of life; the English adjective the KJV uses for both the grave and the unregenerate estate.

Usage

"Dead in trespasses and sins — spiritual death is inability, not a mood; God quickens the dead."

"Dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God — union with Christ changes dominion; it is not the annihilation of the body."

"Faith without works is dead; a church may have a name that it lives and be dead; the dead shall be raised and judged."
